nameStory: The New England cottontail gets its name from its fluffy white tail that looks just like a cotton ball, especially when it's held upright as the rabbit bounds away. The "New England" part distinguishes it from its cousins - this little rabbit was once common throughout the forests and thickets of New England before European settlement changed the landscape.
description: The New England cottontail is a medium-sized rabbit with grayish-brown fur and that classic puffy white tail. They're about the size of a small house cat, weighing 2-3 pounds with large hind feet perfect for quick getaways. These native New Englanders have shorter ears than jackrabbits and compact, rounded bodies built for darting through dense brush. Unfortunately, they're now quite rare - you're much more likely to spot their more common cousin, the Eastern cottontail.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Coarse, grizzled grayish-brown fur with a rusty patch on the nape of the neck that feels rough to the touch, like a wire brush. The belly is white and surprisingly soft.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact rabbit about 15-17 inches long with a rounded, chunky body. Ears are proportionally shorter than an Eastern cottontail's, and the hind legs are powerful and muscular.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four-toed prints in a classic hopping pattern - two large oval hind prints ahead of two smaller round front prints. Hind tracks are about 3 inches long in soft soil.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Freezes motionless when threatened, then explodes into a zigzag sprint through thick brush. More likely to stay hidden in dense cover than venture into open areas.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small, round, marble-sized droppings scattered near feeding areas. Look for clean-cut stems where they've nibbled woody plants - the cuts look like they were made with tiny scissors.

habitat: Dense thickets, shrublands, and early successional forests with thick understory vegetation. They need large patches of continuous brushy habitat - at least 12 acres - with shrub wetlands and impenetrable tangles of multiflora rose, greenbrier, and young forest growth. You'll find them in areas that look almost impassable to humans.

seasonality.spring: Most active during dawn and dusk hours, with breeding season beginning. Fresh tracks are easier to spot in soft, muddy soil from snowmelt.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with young rabbits becoming independent. Look for feeding sign on tender shoots and browse marks on woody stems about 12 inches off the ground.
seasonality.fall: Building up fat reserves for winter, spending more time feeding. Fur begins to get thicker and grayer as winter coat develops.
seasonality.winter: Less active but still foraging, especially on warm days. Tracks in snow are your best bet for detection, and their gray-brown winter coat stands out against white snow.

funFact: New England cottontails practice something called "coprophagy" - they actually eat their own soft, nutrient-rich droppings to extract maximum nutrition from tough plant material, essentially digesting their food twice like tiny furry cows!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from the Eastern cottontail in the field - they're so similar that even wildlife biologists often need genetic testing to tell them apart. The rusty neck patch is slightly more prominent on New England cottontails, but this isn't reliable. When in doubt, consider location: Eastern cottontails prefer more open areas while New England cottontails stick to the thickest brush.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of New England's most endangered mammals, having lost 86% of its historic range since 1960. Many people think they're seeing New England cottontails in their backyards, but they're almost certainly looking at the introduced Eastern cottontail, which has largely replaced its native cousin throughout the region.
compareHints: The New England cottontail is extremely similar to the Eastern cottontail, but tends to be slightly grayer overall with a more prominent rusty neck patch. More importantly, they behave differently - New England cottontails are much more secretive and stick to dense cover, while Eastern cottontails will venture into open lawns and fields. New England cottontails also prefer wilder, more continuous forest habitat rather than the suburban edges where Eastern cottontails thrive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern cottontails are significantly more common and adaptable than their rare cousin, the New England cottontail, preferring more open habitats rather than dense early successional forests.
